scenes.visual: Title card 'Pulled From the Top' over a tall redwood silhouette with one BLUE line running from soil to crown. COLOUR MAP (shared by both films, figures and take-homes): xylem and water BLUE (blue droplets), phloem AMBER, sucrose GOLD hexagons, tension RED, air pale GREY; pressure shown as a vertical gauge with a zero line, positive above (amber when phloem), negative below in RED. Symbols on screen: Ψ, Ψ_s, Ψ_p. Every number appears only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: A coast redwood lifts water more than one hundred metres, with no heart or other pump organ. Where does the force come from?
scenes.visual: Camera tilts up a redwood silhouette beside a scale bar reading '100 m'. A BLUE line runs from roots to the top leaves. A crossed-out heart icon sits at the base, then a question mark appears at the crown.
scenes.narration: A coast redwood lifts water more than one hundred metres, with no heart or other pump organ. Where does the force come from?

scenes.tts: Plant biologists track water with one number, its water potential. Pure water at atmospheric pressure is set at zero. Dissolve a solute in open water, and the number drops below zero. Water crossing a membrane moves toward lower water potential.
scenes.caption: Plant biologists track water with one number, its water potential (Ψ). Pure water at atmospheric pressure is set at zero. Dissolve a solute in open water, and the number drops below zero. Water crossing a membrane moves toward lower water potential.
scenes.visual: A beaker of pure BLUE water with a gauge reading 'Ψ = 0 MPa'. GOLD solute dots drop into a second beaker and its gauge needle sinks below zero. A membrane appears between the beakers; BLUE droplets drift across toward the lower reading, arrow labelled 'toward lower Ψ'.
scenes.narration: Plant biologists track water with one number, its water potential (Ψ). Pure water at atmospheric pressure is set at zero. Dissolve a solute in open water, and the number drops below zero. Water crossing a membrane moves toward lower water potential.

scenes.tts: Now line up a plant, with illustrative values. The soil sits a little below zero, the root lower, the leaf lower still. The air sits far below them all.
scenes.visual: A staircase builds beside a plant cartoon, one step at a time: 'soil -0.3', 'root -0.6', 'leaf -1.5' (MPa), then a sudden cliff down to 'air (50% humidity) about -94 MPa'. Label 'illustrative values'. A BLUE droplet rolls down each step.
scenes.narration: Now line up a plant, with illustrative values. The soil sits a little below zero, the root lower, the leaf lower still. The air sits far below them all.

scenes.tts: So water runs downhill all the way. The biggest drop by far is from the leaf to the dry air.
scenes.visual: The cliff edge between 'leaf' and 'air' flashes; a BLUE droplet falls off it and turns into a pale GREY vapour puff. The staircase stays in a corner for the rest of the film.
scenes.narration: So water runs downhill all the way. The biggest drop by far is from the leaf to the dry air.

scenes.tts: Inside a leaf, water evaporates from the wet walls of the mesophyll cells. These inner cells do photosynthesis. The vapour diffuses out to the drier air.
scenes.visual: Zoom into a leaf cross-section: rounded green mesophyll cells with BLUE-film walls around air spaces; pale GREY vapour puffs drift from the walls through a pore to the outside air.
scenes.narration: Inside a leaf, water evaporates from the wet walls of the mesophyll cells. These inner cells do photosynthesis. The vapour diffuses out to the drier air.

scenes.tts: As water leaves, the water still held in the tiny pores of the walls is held more tightly. Its pressure falls below zero. That is tension, a pull.
scenes.visual: Close-up of one wall pore (schematic): a BLUE water surface sits in the pore; as a droplet evaporates, the surface curves deeper. A gauge beside it drops through the zero line and turns RED, label 'Ψ_p below zero: tension'.
scenes.narration: As water leaves, the water still held in the tiny pores of the walls is held more tightly. Its pressure falls below zero. That is tension, a pull.

scenes.tts: Negative pressure means the water is stretched, not squeezed. Picture a sealed syringe full of water, its plunger pulled back. If no bubble forms, the water pulls on the plunger instead of pushing.
scenes.visual: A rigid syringe with a sealed tip, completely full of BLUE water. The plunger is drawn back slightly; the water stays one unbroken body with no bubble. RED arrows show the water pulling inward on the plunger and walls. Label 'stretched, not squeezed (only while no bubble forms)'. Small note: 'a model of tension, not of flow'.
scenes.narration: Negative pressure means the water is stretched, not squeezed. Picture a sealed syringe full of water, its plunger pulled back. If no bubble forms, the water pulls on the plunger instead of pushing.

scenes.tts: Why does the pull not just snap the water? Water molecules cling to each other through hydrogen bonds. This cohesion lets a thin column in a narrow tube be pulled like a rope.
scenes.visual: Inside a narrow tube, a continuous BLUE liquid column made of many water molecules, joined by a changing network of short dashed links labelled 'hydrogen bonds' that keep breaking and re-forming. A RED tension arrow pulls at the top and is passed down the whole column, which rises as one body of liquid, like a rope. Label 'cohesion: a dynamic hydrogen-bond network transmits tension'.
scenes.narration: Why does the pull not just snap the water? Water molecules cling to each other through hydrogen bonds. This cohesion lets a thin column in a narrow tube be pulled like a rope.

scenes.tts: The tubes are xylem cells called tracheids and vessel elements. They are dead when they work, with their contents gone. They leave a hollow pathway from root to leaf.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the stem: stacked hollow BLUE-outlined tubes, narrow ones labelled 'tracheids' and wider ones labelled 'vessel elements', empty inside, forming one continuous path. The BLUE water column slides up through them from root to leaf.
scenes.narration: The tubes are xylem cells called tracheids and vessel elements. They are dead when they work, with their contents gone. They leave a hollow pathway from root to leaf.

scenes.tts: Henry Dixon and John Joly proposed this in the eighteen nineties. Evaporation pulls, cohesion passes the pull down, and the column stays under tension.
scenes.caption: Henry Dixon and John Joly proposed this in the 1890s. Evaporation pulls, cohesion passes the pull down, and the column stays under tension.
scenes.visual: Caption card 'Dixon and Joly, 1890s: cohesion-tension'. Three icons light up in order along the tree: GREY vapour puff at the leaf, BLUE water column in the stem, RED gauge below zero.
scenes.narration: Henry Dixon and John Joly proposed this in the 1890s. Evaporation pulls, cohesion passes the pull down, and the column stays under tension.

scenes.tts: Height adds a cost. Each metre takes about a hundredth of a megapascal more tension, just to hold a still column. At the top of a one hundred and ten metre redwood, gravity alone adds over one megapascal.
scenes.caption: Height adds a cost. Each metre takes about 0.01 MPa more tension, just to hold a still column. At the top of a 110 m redwood, gravity alone adds over 1 MPa.
scenes.visual: A vertical bar grows beside the redwood trunk, filling from the ground up; tick label 'about 0.01 MPa per metre'. At the crown the bar reads '110 m: over 1 MPa', label 'before any flow'.
scenes.narration: Height adds a cost. Each metre takes about 0.01 MPa more tension, just to hold a still column. At the top of a 110 m redwood, gravity alone adds over 1 MPa.

scenes.tts: Roots can push water too, a little. If xylem water were pushed from below, what would happen when you cut it on a sunny afternoon?
scenes.visual: A cartoon root pushes a BLUE column upward with a small amber arrow. A pair of shears approaches the trunk of a sunlit tree. Question card: 'Pushed? What happens at the cut?'
scenes.narration: Roots can push water too, a little. If xylem water were pushed from below, what would happen when you cut it on a sunny afternoon?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Pushed water would spurt out. It does not. Cut the xylem of a transpiring tree and air is drawn in. The water was under tension.
scenes.visual: The shears snip the trunk. A dashed ghost of a BLUE spurt appears and is crossed out. Instead pale GREY air bubbles are sucked into the cut end; the gauge stays RED below zero. Label 'air drawn in: under tension'.
scenes.narration: Pushed water would spurt out. It does not. Cut the xylem of a transpiring tree and air is drawn in. The water was under tension.

scenes.tts: So the force comes from the top. Evaporation lowers the pressure in the leaf, and the water column below is pulled up toward it.
scenes.visual: Full tree again: GREY vapour leaves the crown, the RED gauge at the leaf sits lowest, and the BLUE column glides upward through the trunk. The staircase from the corner pulses once.
scenes.narration: So the force comes from the top. Evaporation lowers the pressure in the leaf, and the water column below is pulled up toward it.

scenes.tts: Water leaves for lower water potential, and the dry air is lowest of all. So the xylem is pulled, not pushed.
scenes.visual: The words 'pulled, not pushed' settle beside the BLUE column, the word 'pulled' in RED. The column keeps rising slowly.
scenes.narration: Water leaves for lower water potential, and the dry air is lowest of all. So the xylem is pulled, not pushed.

scenes.visual: Hex end card with one line only: 'Evaporation lowers the pressure at the top, so xylem water is pulled.'
